memory_candidates.content: On this repo, `generate-context-line-counts.sh --write` and any `deploy-headless.sh` run (it auto-repairs line_count before deploying) resync ALL stale index-entries.json entries in the source store it touches, not just the ones the current task owns -- including entries whose underlying .md files were edited by a DIFFERENT, concurrently-running sibling task/session. Running --write (directly, or via a deploy) during a multi-task orchestration batch will therefore pick up foreign line_count changes every single time. Before committing index-entries.json, always `git diff` it and revert any entry whose owning file is not in the current task's own file_scope, keeping only the entries this task's own edits actually require. A one-off python regex script keyed on each foreign entry's unique `summary` string (not file path, since multiple entries can share a path prefix) is a reliable way to do this repeatedly across many redeploys within one dispatch.

Two files on this repo (orchestrate-batch-admit.sh, orchestrate-triage-classify.sh) are audited per-line by lint-json-channel-discipline.sh with a strict 'exactly one unredirected printf/echo in the whole file is the legitimate final JSON emit' rule. Adding ANY new printf/echo-based helper -- even a local degrade-safe fallback function whose output is only ever captured via `$(...)` command substitution and never actually reaches the script's real stdout -- trips this as a second unredirected write, a false positive the lint's static per-line scan cannot distinguish from a genuine leak. Fix: compute the needed string into a plain variable via an if/else (checking `declare -F fn` and branching) with NO printf/echo token on either branch, rather than defining a local fallback function. The call site then interpolates the variable directly instead of calling a function.

A new shell test file created via the Write tool does not carry an executable bit (mode 644), and run-all.sh silently [SKIP]s a non-executable scripts/tests/test-*.sh file rather than failing loudly -- the suite simply never runs, with no red signal. After creating a new test file, always `chmod +x` it and verify via `ls -la` (both the source-store copy and, after redeploying, the deployed copy) before relying on `run-all.sh --only <name>` to have actually exercised it; a [PASS]/[FAIL] line in run-all.sh output does not by itself prove the file ran -- check for a [SKIP] line with 'not executable' too.
